common_name: Ishii's Toad Lily (White Unspotted Bell-Flowered Species)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring into moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; this species prefers a cooler, more sheltered site than common garden toad lilies.

directions: Plant divisions in spring into consistently moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, ideally in a sheltered woodland setting that mimics its native rocky Japanese forest habitat. Unlike most toad lilies, Tricyrtis ishiiana bears clean white, bell-shaped flowers with little to no purple spotting, making it a striking contrast to the heavily speckled hybrids and cultivars more commonly grown. Keep soil evenly moist through summer and avoid letting the shallow root mass dry out, as this species is less tolerant of drought stress than T. hirta or T. formosana. It is slower to form large clumps, so leave it undisturbed for several seasons before dividing.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring into gritty, humus-rich, well-drained soil in light to partial shade; good drainage is essential since this alpine species resents winter wet more than other Tricyrtis.

directions: Plant divisions in spring into gritty, humus-rich, sharply drained soil in light to partial shade, such as a raised bed, trough, or rock garden pocket. Tricyrtis nana is a true alpine dwarf from Japan's high mountains, forming a tight clump only a few inches tall yet producing flowers disproportionately large for its stature, typically pale yellow with little spotting in late summer to fall. This species is the compact parent behind several dwarf yellow-flowered toad lily hybrids, so growing the species itself lets gardeners see the diminutive scale that breeders have worked from. Protect from standing winter moisture and avoid heavy, water-retentive soils that cause crown rot.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring into moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; this rare island species needs consistently humid conditions and is best suited to milder, warm-temperate climates.

directions: Plant divisions in spring into consistently moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, choosing a warm, sheltered site since this species comes from subtropical island forests and has limited cold tolerance. Tricyrtis perfoliata is named for its distinctive stem-clasping leaves, which wrap fully around the stem so that the stem appears to pierce straight through the leaf blade, giving the whole plant a layered, architectural look even before the pale, purple-spotted flowers open in fall. Because its native range is extremely restricted, this species is uncommon in cultivation and best treated as a specialty collector's plant rather than a mainstream border perennial. Maintain high humidity and even moisture, and avoid exposing it to drying wind or direct afternoon sun.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring into moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; native to Himalayan forest understories, it tolerates a somewhat wider temperature range than Japanese Tricyrtis species.

directions: Plant divisions in spring into moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, giving the arching, softly hairy stems room to spread. Tricyrtis pilosa takes its name from the fine downy hairs covering its stems and leaves, a texture that distinguishes it at a glance from the smoother-leaved Japanese species, and it bears the typical purple-spotted, orchid-like flowers in leaf axils from late summer into fall. Native across the Himalayan foothills from Nepal through northeastern India into southwestern China, it is adapted to monsoon-influenced moisture patterns, so even summer watering with a slight dry-down in winter suits it well. Divide congested clumps every few years in spring to maintain vigorous flowering.
